title: Mexico-China: Hope
author: La Jornada Editorial Board
content:
_This article by[La Jornada Editorial
Board](https://www.jornada.com.mx/autores/La%20Jornada) originally appeared in
the [November 19, 2026 edition of La
Jornada](https://www.jornada.com.mx/noticia/2026/11/19/editorial/mexicochina-
esperanza), Mexico's premier left wing daily newspaper._

President Claudia Sheinbaum Pardo’s presence at the Asia-Pacific Economic
Cooperation (APEC) summit in Shenzhen, China, has meant a relaunch of
bilateral ties at the highest level, thanks to her meeting with her
counterpart Xi Jinping and the many working meetings held by her and her team.
In this regard, the size and seniority of the delegation that traveled to the
Pearl River Bay reflect the importance the federal government places on the
forum and on relations with Beijing: there are Secretaries Marcelo Ebrard
Casaubón (Economy), Roberto Velasco Álvarez (Foreign Affairs), David
Kershenobich Stalnikowitz (Health), Alicia Bárcena Ibarra (Environment), Luz
Elena González Escobar (Energy), Rosaura Ruiz Gutiérrez (Science, Humanities,
Technology and Innovation), and Josefina Rodríguez Zamora (Tourism), as well
as several undersecretaries.

The officials did not go there to pose for photographs; each is responsible
for an area in which the National Palace seeks to build or strengthen
cooperation with the Asian giant that benefits Mexico. Because of President
Sheinbaum’s visit to the People’s Hospital in Nanshan District, health was the
most discussed aspect of the trip. The hospital’s name could be misleading
because of the association of the term “people’s” with underfunded
institutions used exclusively by lower-income groups, but Nanshan Hospital is
the opposite of that image: it has the world’s most advanced medical
equipment, artificial intelligence assists with diagnoses and prescriptions,
and robots deliver drugs to patients. Far from a blind futurism in which
digitalization serves as a commercial lure, this center is part of a public
health system in which the most advanced technology is combined with
traditional medicine. This is the model of interest to bring to our country,
because it shows **how prevention, modernity and the knowledge of Indigenous
peoples complement one another**.

It was also agreed to explore opportunities for collaboration in technological
development, artificial intelligence, academic and scientific exchanges, clean
energy, water management, river cleanup and combating sargassum, as well as
the possible participation of Chinese companies in railway projects and the
manufacturing of small vehicles, all within the framework of Plan México. As
already mentioned in this space, agriculture played a central role, both
because of the potential of Chinese machinery to modernize Mexico’s
countryside and because **closing the trade deficit gap with agricultural
products** is seen as beneficial. In his keynote address to summit guests,
President Xi referred several times to his government’s interest in increasing
imports of “quality products,” opening the door to Mexican agricultural
exports of high value, such as avocados and tequila.

Bringing these projects to fruition depends on follow-up between officials on
both sides, but merely proposing them is promising for Mexico: as it
strengthens its relationship with the world’s second economic power –and the
first in growing areas of science and technology– our country will have more
and better tools for its development and, no less importantly, to **resist the
pressures, extortion, abuses and outrages that characterize Washington** , our
neighbor and unavoidable trading partner.
